paras: The killing of Julius Hurt was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a local officer, William Jones, at Campbellsville, Kentucky, on November 27, 1882. Jones said Hurt had resisted arrest on a bench warrant, and he was acquitted at an examining trial the same day. A short dispatch about the killing ran in papers from Washington to California, one of which counted it as Kentucky's "daily murder."

According to the Campbellsville special, Jones tried to arrest Hurt, "a colored man," on a bench warrant whose charge was not given. The dispatch said Hurt resisted and "defied him to attempt to arrest him," and that Jones then shot and killed him. A Missouri brief placed the shooting on Monday evening, while the dispatch itself said only "to-day." The papers name neither where in town it happened nor any witnesses, and no account from Hurt's side appears.

Jones was arrested by the town marshal, given an examining trial, and acquitted, all within the same dispatch. A Hopkinsville paper's Kentucky roundup a week later called him "Deputy Marshal Wm. Jones" and said he killed Hurt "for resisting arrest." No report of an inquest or any later proceeding was found.

Every account goes back to one Campbellsville special, which several papers credited to the Louisville Courier-Journal. It appeared on November 28 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Washington National Republican, the Wheeling Register, the Las Vegas Daily Gazette and the Dallas Daily Herald, and later in the Dallas Weekly Herald and the Kirksville Weekly Graphic. Most headlines framed the killing in the officer's terms, as "Killed While Resisting an Officer" or "Shot By An Officer," and repeated the resistance claim as fact.

The Washington National Republican ran the same text under the heading "The Daily Murder in Kentucky," grouping it with the state's homicides rather than with routine arrests. The victim's surname was printed as both Hart and Hurt, and the Kentucky paper and most Courier-Journal copies used Hurt.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch unchanged under headlines such as 'Killed While Resisting an Officer', 'Killed by an Officer' and 'Shot By An Officer', taking the resistance claim as fact.
The Washington National Republican printed the same text under the heading 'The Daily Murder in Kentucky', placing it among the state's killings.

conflicts.note: The same dispatch carries both spellings; the Kentucky paper (A8) and most Courier-Journal copies print Hurt, so Hurt is slightly better supported.
Not contradictory; the Kentucky roundup gives a more specific title.
